definition: The smallest unit of an element: a tiny, dense nucleus surrounded by an electron cloud, about 0.1–0.5 nm across.
The central core of an atom, made of protons and neutrons; only femtometers across, it holds more than 99.9% of the atom's mass.
10⁻¹⁵ m, the natural length unit for nuclei; a proton's charge radius is about 0.84 fm.
0.0529 nm: the most probable distance of hydrogen's ground-state electron from the nucleus, and the radius of the n = 1 orbit in the Bohr model.
A three-dimensional standing-wave pattern of an electron in an atom; its square gives the probability of finding the electron at each point.
The mathematical wave that describes a quantum particle; its square is the probability density.
A picture of an orbital's probability density as shading; it fades smoothly with distance and has no hard edge.
The wavelength of a moving particle, λ = h/(mv); for an electron in hydrogen's ground state it is 0.332 nm.
A wave pattern confined to a region, such as a plucked string, that vibrates in place; only certain wavelengths fit the boundaries.
The restriction of a quantity, such as a bound electron's energy, to certain discrete values; it arises because confined waves allow only certain patterns.
One of the allowed energies of an electron bound in an atom or molecule; for hydrogen, E_n = −13.6 eV/n².
The whole number 1, 2, 3, … that labels hydrogen's energy levels and sets their energy and size.
The lowest-energy state of an atom (n = 1 for hydrogen), where an undisturbed atom normally sits.
Any state above the ground state; an atom gets there by absorbing energy and usually leaves within nanoseconds.
The minimum energy needed to remove the most loosely held electron from an isolated ground-state atom; 13.6 eV for hydrogen, 3.89–24.6 eV across the elements.
An atom (or molecule) that has lost or gained electrons and so carries a net electric charge.
No two electrons can occupy the same quantum state; it forces overlapping electron clouds into higher energies and helps make matter solid.
The distance between neighboring nuclei at which attraction and repulsion balance, typically 0.2–0.3 nm in solids; it sets the atomic radius used in crystal models.
